extracted.intended_audience: AI/ML researchers, practitioners, and policymakers interested in the capabilities, evaluation, and societal impacts of large language models (e.g., GPT-4)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and desiderata for assessing the capabilities, limitations, architecture needs, and societal implications of large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4, and for guiding future research and system design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for machine automation (task rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks considered suitable for automation were those having well-defined inputs and outputs and availability or ease of creating datasets for tasks with input-output pairs. The original rubric (BM17) mapped occupations to tasks and assigned each task a 'suitability for machine learning'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that advent of powerful LLMs like GPT-4 may change which attributes matter for automation; criteria that applied to supervised ML may no longer fully apply. Use task decomposition into input-output clarity and dataset availability as a starting point, but re-evaluate in light of models that handle broader, less-structured tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human–AI complementarity and collaboration principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Design should consider the complementarity of human and machine contributions, including timing and content of machine interventions, shaping ML procedures for maximal human value, and considering human mental models as systems evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow core principles from research on mixed-initiative systems: assess where AI adds value vs where humans should remain in the loop; design for ideal timing/content of AI contributions; provide oversight and tooling for human guidance. References include work on mixed-initiative UI, updating in human-AI teams, and guided exploration of unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access and equity (avoid an 'AI divide')
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether powerful AI capabilities are available only to privileged groups — limited access may amplify societal divides across demographics, countries, and sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deploying or funding systems, weigh tradeoffs between sharing state-of-the-art capabilities and mitigating risks; consider policies or investments to create opportunity for historically marginalized communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy and confidentiality protections
rubrics_metrics.description: High-fidelity, expressive engagements with general AI systems increase demands for confidentiality and privacy assurances; people and organizations may request private instances or protection against logging/leakage or inferential privacy risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide mechanisms (e.g., private instances, logging controls) and consider risks from memorization or inferential leakage. Build product and policy layers to address requests for private deployments and data protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and attribution of human vs machine contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be interest or calls for marking the origin of content (human versus machine or mixed) to mitigate confusion, deception, or harm regarding use and type of content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support provenance metadata and mechanisms for marking training contributions and outputs; enable users to control whether their content is used for training and how contributions are attributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation beyond classical benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Move evaluation beyond structured dataset benchmarking; evaluation of broad LLM capabilities should become closer in essence to evaluating human cognitive abilities rather than narrow AI tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop formal, comprehensive methods for testing reasoning, planning, learning-from-experience, and other human-like cognitive abilities. Use interactive, open-ended, multi-domain evaluations and consider both depth and generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: AGI/evidence criteria (what counts as general intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper treats evidence for general intelligence as demonstration of core mental capabilities (reasoning, creativity, deduction), breadth of topics of expertise, and variety of tasks the model can perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming AGI-like behavior, assess (a) reasoning and planning abilities, (b) creative problem solving, (c) ability across many domains (medicine, literature, coding, etc.), and (d) multiplicity of task types (games, tool use, explanations). Recognize these as suggestive rather than sufficient for full AGI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: The model struggles to know when to be confident vs when it is guessing; it can make up facts (hallucinate) and present them persuasively, leading to errors and mistrust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include: improve calibration via prompting or fine-tuning so the model abstains or signals low confidence; allow model to call external sources (search, tools) to reduce open-domain hallucination; use post-hoc checks for closed-domain hallucination; design UX to account for possible hallucinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term memory / evolving context
rubrics_metrics.description: The model is effectively stateless with limited context; there is no easy way for it to learn new facts or maintain evolving context needed for tasks like following a book across chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate mechanisms for persistent memory or context vectors that accompany input/output so the model can maintain and use long-term information across sessions and over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continual learning (online/adaptive updates)
rubrics_metrics.description: The model lacks the ability to update itself or adapt to a changing environment without full retraining; fine-tuning on new data can cause degradation or overfitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop methods for safe continual learning that incorporate new information and feedback without catastrophic forgetting or performance degradation; explore architectures and training protocols that permit incremental updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization and organizational adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some applications require tailoring to an organization or individual (preferences, workflows, learning styles); current methods (meta-prompts) are limited and inefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide mechanisms for persistent personalization that adapt over time (e.g., user models, organizational knowledge bases) and allow efficient, safe customization without compromising general performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning and conceptual leaps
rubrics_metrics.description: The model has difficulty on tasks requiring forward planning or discontinuous conceptual leaps (the kind of 'Eureka idea' that advances progress toward a solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate planning ability explicitly (multi-step tasks requiring foresight); research architectures that combine fast next-token prediction with mechanisms enabling higher-level planning and conceptual abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, interpretability, and self-consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The model may hallucinate and produce inconsistent content, and post-hoc explanations are only useful when they accurately reflect the process that produced the decision; verifying such explanations is hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require mechanisms to verify consistency between outputs and explanations; invest in interpretability tools, verifiers, and procedures that can check internal reasoning or cross-check outputs against sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive biases and irrationality
rubrics_metrics.description: The model exhibits limitations akin to human cognitive biases (confirmation bias, anchoring, base-rate neglect) and may inherit prejudices present in training data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and mitigate systematic biases through data curation, debiasing methods, adversarial testing, and human oversight. Include bias tests and social-impact analyses in evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and sensitivity to inputs (prompt robustness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses can be highly sensitive to subtle details of prompt framing and sequencing; non-robustness requires significant prompt engineering to achieve good results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include robustness checks in evaluation (paraphrase prompts, reorder instructions, vary context) and develop methods to make models less prompt-sensitive or to provide reliable prompt design guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural extensions as desiderata (tools and slow-thinking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential extensions beyond pure next-token prediction could include: (1) allowing external calls to tools (calculators, search, code execution); (2) a slow-thinking deeper mechanism overseeing fast next-token prediction for planning/verification; (3) integration of long-term memory vectors in I/O; (4) hierarchical generation over sentences/paragraphs/ideas rather than only tokens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these architectural changes as evaluation axes: measure whether such extensions improve planning, verification, memory, and reduction of hallucination. Investigate whether large-scale next-token training suffices or whether these structural changes are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing RLHF artifacts from architectural limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some drawbacks may be due to how reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) was applied rather than inherent to next-token architectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing failures (e.g., hallucination), compare variants with different RLHF procedures on the same architecture to separate training-policy artifacts from architectural limitations.
